name: Mongolian royal red cheek spots

card.summary: A historical cosmetic custom in which royal women reportedly painted red spots on the cheeks below the eyes, a blush that accentuated the cheekbones.
card.note: Historical practice with very thin documentation; the reason for it is recorded as unclear.

quick.overview:
Women of royal families in Mongolia are reported to have painted red spots in the centre of the cheeks, just under the eyes. It is an early form of blush, and the effect is a flushed, defined cheekbone area.

The record is brief. One encyclopedia entry notes the reason for the custom is unclear, while blush in general was seen as a sign of a happy queen and a way to emphasise the cheekbones.
quick.how: In practice the look is a small, round or dab-shaped patch of red placed high on the cheek beneath the eye, rather than blended outward. Modern makeup artists reproduce the idea with cream blush placed on the cheekbone.
quick.risks: Modern cosmetic risk is low (skin reactions to colourants). Historical pigments used are not documented in the accounts consulted.

lead: According to a history of cosmetics summary, women of royal families in Mongolia painted red spots at the centre of the cheeks, right under the eyes.[1] The same account says the reason is unclear, and that blush was regarded as a sign of a happy queen and as a way to accentuate the cheekbones.[1]

The source gives no date, and a search of material on medieval Mongolian women's dress turns up descriptions of hair, headdresses (boqta) and robes but no mention of cheek colouring.[2] The practice is therefore recorded in a single short general reference.

chain: Red spot painted high on cheek
Colour draws the eye to the cheekbone
Face looks flushed and more defined
angle.text: Colour placed on the cheekbones adds the appearance of vitality and highlights facial structure, the same logic behind modern blush.

infobox: Centre of cheek, under the eyes

paras: The custom is described as red spots on the middle of the cheek directly beneath the eye.[1] Blush has also been read as a signal of a happy queen, and as a way to bring out the cheekbones.[1]

Mongol women of the Yuan and Ilkhanid periods are documented in art with looped braids, long braids with jewellery, and tall decorated boqta headdresses; Friar William of Rubruck recorded in the early 1250s that married women shaved the front of the head.[2] These accounts focus on upper-class women and do not describe facial makeup.[2]
Rouge was widespread in other eras and regions, for example in medieval Europe, where faces were whitened and cheeks rouged.[1]
